content.heading: 4.8 Applications to Difference Equations
content.paragraph: Continuing our study of discrete-time signals, in this section we explore difference equations, a valuable tool used to filter the data contained in signals. Even when a differential equation is used to model a continuous process, a numerical solution is often produced from a related difference equation. This section highlights some fundamental properties of linear difference equations that are explained using linear algebra.

content.paragraph: If a Casorati matrix is not invertible, the associated signals being tested may or may not be linearly dependent. (See Exercise 35.) However, it can be shown that if the signals are all solutions of the same homogeneous difference equation (described below), then either the Casorati matrix is invertible for all $k$ and the signals are linearly independent, or else the Casorati matrix is not invertible for all $k$ and the signals are linearly dependent. A nice proof using linear transformations is in the Study Guide.
content.heading: Linear Difference Equations
content.paragraph: Given scalars $a_{0},\ldots\text{,~}a_{n}$, with $a_{0}$ and $a_{n}$ nonzero, and given a signal $\{ z_{k}\}$, the equation

paragraph.math: $$a_{0}y_{k + n} + a_{1}y_{k + n - 1} + \cdots + a_{n - 1}y_{k + 1} + a_{n}y_{k} = z_{k}\quad\text{for all~}k$$

content.paragraph: is called a linear difference equation (or linear recurrence relation) of order $n$. For simplicity, $a_{0}$ is often taken equal to 1. If $\{ z_{k}\}$ is the zero sequence, the equation is homogeneous; otherwise, the equation is nonhomogeneous.

In digital signal processing (DSP), a difference equation such as (3) describes a linear time invariant (LTI) filter, and $a_{0}\text{,}\ldots\text{,~}a_{n}$ are called the filter coefficients. content.heading: Solution Sets of Linear Difference Equations
content.paragraph: Given $a_{1}\text{,}\ldots\text{,~}a_{n}$, recall that the LTI transformation $\left. T:\mathbb{S}\rightarrow\mathbb{S} \right.$ given by
transforms a signal $\{ y_{k}\}$ into the signal $\{ w_{k}\}$ given by

paragraph.math: $$w_{k} = y_{k + n} + a_{1}y_{k + n - 1} + \cdots + a_{n - 1}y_{k + 1} + a_{n}y_{k}\text{\quad for all~}k$$

content.paragraph: This implies that the solution set of the homogeneous equation

paragraph.math: $$y_{k + n} + a_{1}y_{k + n - 1} + \cdots + a_{n - 1}y_{k + 1} + a_{n}y_{k} = 0\text{\quad for all~}k$$

content.paragraph: is the kernel of $T$ and describes the signals that are filtered out or transformed into the zero signal. Since the kernel of any linear transformation with domain $\mathbb{S}$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{S}$, so is the solution set of a homogeneous equation. Any linear combination of solutions is again a solution.
The next theorem, a simple but basic result, will lead to more information about the solution sets of difference equations.

note.title: Theorem 20
note.heading: Theorem 20
note.paragraph: The set $H$ of all solutions of the $n\text{th-order}$ homogeneous linear difference equation

paragraph.math: $$y_{k + n} + a_{1}y_{k + n - 1} + \cdots + a_{n - 1}y_{k + 1} + a_{n}y_{k} = 0\quad\text{for all~}k$$

content.heading: Proof
content.paragraph: As was pointed out earlier, $H$ is a subspace of $\mathbf{\mathbb{S}}$ because $H$ is the kernel of a linear transformation. For $\{ y_{k}\}$ in $H$, let $F\{ y_{k}\}$ be the vector in $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ given by $\left( y_{0}\text{,~}y_{1}\text{,}\ldots\text{,~}y_{n - 1} \right)$. It is readily verified that $\left. F:H\rightarrow\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n} \right.$ is a linear transformation. Given any vector $\left( y_{0}\text{,~}y_{1}\text{,}\ldots\text{,~}y_{n - 1} \right)$ in $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$, Theorem 19 says that there is a unique signal $\{ y_{k}\}$ in $H$ such that $F\left\{ y_{k} \right\} = \left( y_{0}\text{,~}y_{1}\text{,}\ldots\text{,~}y_{n - 1} \right)$. This means that $F$ is a one-to-one linear transformation of $H$ onto $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$; that is, $F$ is an isomorphism. Thus $\text{dim~}H = \text{dim~}\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n} = n$. (See Exercise 52 in Section 4.5.)

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Find a basis for the set of all solutions to the difference equation
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Our work in linear algebra really pays off now! We know from Examples 1 and 3 that $\{ 1^{k}\}$, $\{( - 2)^{k}\}$, and $\{ 3^{k}\}$ are linearly independent solutions. In general, it can be difficult to verify directly that a set of signals spans the solution space. But that is no problem here because of two key theorems—Theorem 20, which shows that the solution space is exactly three-dimensional, and the Basis Theorem in Section 4.5, which says that a linearly independent set of $n$ vectors in an $n\text{-dimensional}$ space is automatically a basis. So $\{ 1^{k}\}$, $\{( - 2)^{k}\}$, and $\{ 3^{k}\}$ form a basis for the solution space.

content.paragraph: The standard way to describe the “general solution” of the difference equation (10) is to exhibit a basis for the subspace of all solutions. Such a basis is usually called a fundamental set of solutionsof (10). In practice, if you can find $n$ linearly independent signals that satisfy (10), they will automatically span the $n\text{-dimensional}$ solution space, as explained in Example 4.
content.heading: Nonhomogeneous Equations
content.paragraph: The general solution of the nonhomogeneous difference equation

paragraph.math: $$y_{k + n} + a_{1}y_{k + n - 1} + \cdots + a_{n - 1}y_{k + 1} + a_{n}y_{k} = z_{k}\quad\text{for all~}k$$

content.paragraph: can be written as one particular solution of (11) plus an arbitrary linear combination of a fundamental set of solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation (10). This fact is analogous to the result in Section 1.5 showing that the solution sets of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ and $A\mathbf{x} = 0$ are parallel. Both results have the same explanation: The mapping $\left. \mathbf{x}\mapsto{A\mathbf{x}} \right.$ is linear, and the mapping that transforms the signal $\{ y_{k}\}$ into the signal $\{ z_{k}\}$ in (11) is linear.

When a signal is produced from a sequence of measurements made on a process (a chemical reaction, a flow of heat through a tube, a moving robot arm, etc.), the signal usually contains random noise produced by measurement errors. A standard method of preprocessing the data to reduce the noise is to smooth or filter the data. One simple filter is a moving average that replaces each $y_{k}$ by its average with the two adjacent values:$\frac{1}{3}y_{k + 1} + \frac{1}{3}y_{k} + \frac{1}{3}y_{k - 1} = z_{k} {for}k = 1,2,\ldots$
